pumac-2011-power-ex09.title: Convexity
pumac-2011-power-ex09.body:
Let $\ell$ be the line through $D,E,F$ and $T$ the closed triangular region $ABC$. The line $\ell$ contains no vertex: if it contained, say, $A$, then $E=\ell\cap AC=A$ (or $\ell=AC$ and then $D=\ell\cap BC=C$), contradicting distinctness; similarly for $B,C$. Also $\ell$ is not a side line. So $D,E,F$ are exactly the intersection points of $\ell$ with the three side lines.

$T$ is convex, so $\ell\cap T$ is empty, a single point, or a segment. A single point would have to be a vertex (a line through a point of the boundary which is not a vertex either contains a boundary segment or enters the interior), excluded. So $\ell\cap T$ is empty or a nondegenerate segment, whose two endpoints are the only points of $\ell$ on the boundary of $T$. A point of $\ell$ on the boundary lies on exactly one side segment (no vertices) and is the corresponding one of $D,E,F$. Hence the number of the points $D,E,F$ lying on their side segments is $0$ or $2$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex08.title: Distances to $d$
pumac-2011-power-ex08.body: Let $h_i$ be the distance from $A_i$ to $d$ (assume the $M_i$ are distinct from the vertices so no denominator vanishes). The line $A_iA_{i+1}$ meets $d$ at $M_i$; the points $A_i,A_{i+1}$ lie on this line at distances $M_iA_i,M_iA_{i+1}$ from $M_i$, and the distance of a point of the line to $d$ is proportional to its distance from $M_i$ (similar right triangles). Hence $\frac{M_iA_i}{M_iA_{i+1}}=\frac{h_i}{h_{i+1}}$ for $i=1,2,3,4$ (indices mod $4$). The product telescopes: $\frac{h_1}{h_2}\cdot\frac{h_2}{h_3}\cdot\frac{h_3}{h_4}\cdot\frac{h_4}{h_1}=1$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex08.title: Via the diagonal
pumac-2011-power-ex08.body: Let $M$ be the intersection of $d$ with the diagonal $A_1A_3$. Menelaus in $\triangle A_1A_2A_3$ (transversal $M_1,M_2,M$): $\frac{M_1A_1}{M_1A_2}\cdot\frac{M_2A_2}{M_2A_3}\cdot\frac{MA_3}{MA_1}=1$; in $\triangle A_1A_3A_4$ (transversal $M,M_3,M_4$): $\frac{M_3A_3}{M_3A_4}\cdot\frac{M_4A_4}{M_4A_1}\cdot\frac{MA_1}{MA_3}=1$. Multiply. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex07a.title: Ceva
pumac-2011-power-ex07a.body: $\frac{AF}{FB}\cdot\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}=1\cdot1\cdot1=1$ and all three points lie on the segments, so by Ceva's theorem $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex07b.title: Angle bisector theorem and Ceva
pumac-2011-power-ex07b.body: By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{c}{b}$, $\frac{CE}{EA}=\frac{a}{c}$, $\frac{AF}{FB}=\frac{b}{a}$. Their product is $\frac cb\cdot\frac ac\cdot\frac ba=1$, and $D,E,F$ lie on the segments. By Ceva, $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex06a.title: Mass points
pumac-2011-power-ex06a.body:
Put masses $\mu(A),\mu(B),\mu(C)$ with $\mu(A)\cdot AF=\mu(B)\cdot FB$, i.e. $\mu(A):\mu(B)=3:2$, and $\mu(B)\cdot BD=\mu(C)\cdot DC$, i.e. $\mu(B):\mu(C)=5:1$. Take $\mu(B)=10$: $\mu(A)=15$, $\mu(C)=2$. $E$ is the centre of mass of $A,C$: $\mu(A)\cdot AE=\mu(C)\cdot CE$, so $\frac{AE}{CE}=\frac{2}{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac2{15}$**

pumac-2011-power-ex06b.title: Mass points
pumac-2011-power-ex06b.body:
With masses $15,10,2$ at $A,B,C$ (see part (a)), $D$ has mass $\mu(B)+\mu(C)=12$ and $X$ is the centre of mass of $A$ and $D$: $15\cdot AX=12\cdot XD$, so $\frac{AX}{XD}=\frac45$ and $\frac{AX}{AD}=\frac49$, i.e. $\frac{AD}{AX}=\frac94$.

**Answer: $\frac94$**

pumac-2011-power-ex06b.title: Menelaus
pumac-2011-power-ex06b.body:
Apply Menelaus to $\triangle ABD$ with the transversal $F,X,C$ ($F\in AB$, $X\in AD$, $C\in BD$): $\frac{AF}{FB}\cdot\frac{BC}{CD}\cdot\frac{DX}{XA}=1$, i.e. $\frac23\cdot\frac65\cdot\frac{DX}{XA}=1$, so $\frac{DX}{XA}=\frac54$ and $\frac{AD}{AX}=\frac{AX+XD}{AX}=1+\frac54=\frac94$.

**Answer: $\frac94$**

pumac-2011-power-ex06c.title: Areas via masses
pumac-2011-power-ex06c.body:
Let $[ABC]=T$. The areas of $\triangle BXC,\triangle CXA,\triangle AXB$ are proportional to the masses at $A,B,C$, i.e. to $15:10:2$ (total $27$): $[BXC]=\frac{15}{27}T$, $[AXB]=\frac2{27}T$. Triangles $AFX$ and $ABX$ share the height from $X$, so $[AFX]=\frac{AF}{AB}[AXB]=\frac25\cdot\frac2{27}T=\frac4{135}T$. Similarly $[CDX]=\frac{CD}{CB}[CXB]=\frac56\cdot\frac{15}{27}T=\frac{25}{54}T$. The ratio is $\frac{4/135}{25/54}=\frac{4\cdot54}{135\cdot25}=\frac{8}{125}$.

**Answer: $\frac8{125}$**

pumac-2011-power-ex06c.title: Coordinates
pumac-2011-power-ex06c.body:
Take $A=(0,0)$, $B=(5,0)$, $C=(0,6)$ (the ratio of areas is affine invariant). Then $F=(2,0)$ and $D=B+\frac16(C-B)=\left(\frac{25}6,1\right)$. The line $AD$ is $t\left(\frac{25}6,1\right)$ and the line $CF$ is $(2u,6-6u)$; equating, $\frac{25}6(6-6u)=2u$, so $u=\frac{25}{27}$ and $X=\left(\frac{50}{27},\frac49\right)$. Then $[AFX]=\frac12\cdot AF\cdot y_X=\frac12\cdot2\cdot\frac49=\frac49$ and by the shoelace formula $[CDX]=\frac12\left|\frac{25}6\left(\frac49-6\right)+\frac{50}{27}(6-1)\right|=\frac{125}{18}$. The ratio is $\frac49\cdot\frac{18}{125}=\frac8{125}$.

**Answer: $\frac8{125}$**

pumac-2011-power-ex05.title: Vectors
pumac-2011-power-ex05.body:
Put $\vec u=B-A$, $\vec v=C-A$ (linearly independent). From $A'B'\parallel AB$: $B'-A'=\lambda\vec u$; from $A'C'\parallel AC$: $C'-A'=\mu\vec v$. Then $C'-B'=\mu\vec v-\lambda\vec u$ must be parallel to $C-B=\vec v-\vec u$: $\mu\vec v-\lambda\vec u=
u(\vec v-\vec u)$, so by independence $\mu=
u=\lambda=:k$. Hence the map $\varphi(X)=A'+k(X-A)$ sends $A,B,C$ to $A',B',C'$.

If $k=1$, $\varphi$ is a translation, so $AA',BB',CC'$ are parallel (all equal to the same vector). If $k
e1$, $\varphi$ is a homothety with a centre $O$ ($O=\varphi(O)$: $O= rac{A'-kA}{1-k}$); the centre of a homothety lies on the line joining every point to its image, so $O$ lies on $AA',BB',CC'$: they are concurrent. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex04.title: Pascal
pumac-2011-power-ex04.body:
Apply Pascal to the hexagon $F,F,D,D,E,E$ inscribed in the incircle (consecutive equal points mean tangents): $A_1=A_2=F$, $A_3=A_4=D$, $A_5=A_6=E$.
* $A_1A_2\cap A_4A_5$: the tangent at $F$ (which is $AB$) meets $DE$ in $X$.
* $A_2A_3\cap A_5A_6$: the line $FD$ meets the tangent at $E$ (which is $CA$) in $Z$.
* $A_3A_4\cap A_6A_1$: the tangent at $D$ (which is $BC$) meets $EF$ in $Y$.

By Pascal these three points are collinear. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex03.title: Coordinate along the line
pumac-2011-power-ex03.body:
$A,B,C$ lie on the line $y=x-1$; write the point $(1+t,t)$ as the number $t$. Then $A=0$, $C=3$, $B=4$. For four points with coordinates $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$ in this order, harmonic means $\frac{P_2P_1}{P_2P_3}=\frac{P_4P_1}{P_4P_3}$ (as lengths).

* $(ACBD)$: $\frac{CA}{CB}=3$, so $\frac{DA}{DB}=3$ with $D$ beyond $B$: $\frac{t}{t-4}=3\Rightarrow t=6$, $D=(7,6)$.
* $(ACEB)$: $\frac{CA}{CE}=\frac{BA}{BE}$ with $E=t$ between $C$ and $B$: $\frac3{t-3}=\frac4{4-t}\Rightarrow12-3t=4t-12\Rightarrow t=\frac{24}7$, $E=\left(\frac{31}7,\frac{24}7\right)$.
* $(AFCB)$: $\frac{FA}{FC}=\frac{BA}{BC}=4$ with $F=t$ between $A$ and $C$: $\frac{t}{3-t}=4\Rightarrow t=\frac{12}5$, $F=\left(\frac{17}5,\frac{12}5\right)$.

pumac-2011-power-ex02.title: Polar of a point
pumac-2011-power-ex02.body:
For $P=(p,q)$ and the circle $x^2+y^2=r^2$, the polar is $px+qy=r^2$: the points $Q$ for which $(PXQY)$ is harmonic satisfy $\vec{OP}\cdot\vec{OQ}=r^2$ (inversion property). Here $r^2=4$, $P=(a,a)$: $ax+ay=4$, i.e. $x+y=\frac4a$.

Check with a line through $P$ towards $O$: the line $y=x$ meets $\Gamma$ at $X,Y=(\pm\sqrt2,\pm\sqrt2)$; the harmonic conjugate $Q$ of $P$ has distance $q$ from $O$ with $q\cdot p=r^2$ along that line, where $p=a\sqrt2$: $q=\frac{4}{a\sqrt2}$, $Q=\left(\frac2a,\frac2a\right)$, which satisfies $x+y=\frac4a$. ✓

**Answer: $x+y=\frac4a$**

pumac-2011-power-ex01a.title: Ceva versus Menelaus
pumac-2011-power-ex01a.body:
$Y,Z$ lie on the segments, so by Menelaus (one or three outside) $X'$ lies outside $BC$ and, since $X',Y,Z$ are collinear, $\frac{X'B}{X'C}\cdot\frac{YC}{YA}\cdot\frac{ZA}{ZB}=1$, i.e. $\frac{X'B}{X'C}=\frac{YA}{YC}\cdot\frac{ZB}{ZA}$.

By Ceva (all three points on the segments), $AX,BY,CZ$ are concurrent iff $\frac{XB}{XC}\cdot\frac{YC}{YA}\cdot\frac{ZA}{ZB}=1$, i.e. iff $\frac{XB}{XC}=\frac{YA}{YC}\cdot\frac{ZB}{ZA}$.

Hence concurrency $\iff\frac{XB}{XC}=\frac{X'B}{X'C}$, which is exactly the statement that $(BXCX')$ is harmonic. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex01b.title: The forward statement
pumac-2011-power-ex01b.body:
For collinear $A,B,C$ and a point $P$ off the line, triangles $PAB$ and $PBC$ have the same height from $P$, so $\frac{BA}{BC}=\frac{[PAB]}{[PBC]}=\frac{PA\,\sin\angle APB}{PC\,\sin\angle BPC}$. Likewise $\frac{DA}{DC}=\frac{PA\,\sin\angle APD}{PC\,\sin\angle DPC}$. Dividing,
$$\frac{BA}{BC}:\frac{DA}{DC}=\frac{\sin\angle APB\cdot\sin\angle DPC}{\sin\angle BPC\cdot\sin\angle APD}.$$
This depends only on the lines $PA,PB,PC,PD$ (replacing a ray by the opposite ray changes an angle to its supplement, with the same sine), so the same expression is obtained for $A',B',C',D'$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-ex01b.title: The converse
pumac-2011-power-ex01b.body:
Take $A$ as origin and use oblique coordinates $(x,y)$ with axes $\ell$ and $\ell'$ (unit vectors along the lines), so $B=(b,0)$, $C=(c,0)$, $D=(d,0)$ and $B'=(0,b')$, $C'=(0,c')$, $D'=(0,d')$ with signed $b,c,d,b',c',d'$. Put $\beta=\frac1b$, $\gamma=\frac1c$, $\delta=\frac1d$ and similarly $\beta',\gamma',\delta'$. The signed cross-ratio is
$$\frac{BA}{BC}:\frac{DA}{DC}=\frac{-b}{c-b}\cdot\frac{c-d}{-d}=\frac{\delta-\gamma}{\beta-\gamma},$$
and for the primed points $\frac{\delta'-\gamma'}{\beta'-\gamma'}$. The line $BB'$ is $\beta x+\beta'y=1$, and similarly $CC'$: $\gamma x+\gamma'y=1$ and $DD'$: $\delta x+\delta'y=1$. These three lines are concurrent or all parallel iff the vectors $(\beta,\beta',-1),(\gamma,\gamma',-1),(\delta,\delta',-1)$ are linearly dependent, i.e. iff the points $(\beta,\beta')$, $(\gamma,\gamma')$, $(\delta,\delta')$ are collinear, i.e. iff $(\delta-\gamma)(\beta'-\gamma')=(\delta'-\gamma')(\beta-\gamma)$, which is precisely the equality of the two cross-ratios. ∎ (The same computation shows that, with $A,B,C$ and $B',C'$ fixed, the cross-ratio determines $D'$ from $D$.)

pumac-2011-power-p1a.title: Newton's theorem
pumac-2011-power-p1a.body:
**Lemma (Newton).** Let $PQRS$ be a convex quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle touching $PQ,QR,RS,SP$ at $K,L,M,N$. Then $PR,QS,KM,LN$ are concurrent.

*Proof.* Let $U=PR\cap LN$. The tangents $RQ$ and $SP$ touch the circle at $L$ and $N$, so $\angle RLN$ and $\angle SNL$ are the tangent–chord angles on the same chord, hence equal; thus $\sin\angle RLU=\sin\angle PNU$ (they are equal or supplementary). The law of sines in $\triangle PNU$ and $\triangle RLU$ gives $\frac{PU}{RU}=\frac{PN\sin\angle PNU/\sin\angle PUN}{RL\sin\angle RLU/\sin\angle RUL}=\frac{PN}{RL}$ (the angles at $U$ are vertical angles with equal sines). Since $PN=PK$ and $RL=RM$ (tangent segments), $\frac{PU}{UR}=\frac{PK}{RL}$. $U$ lies on segment $PR$ (the chord $LN$ joins the opposite sides $QR$, $SP$ and so crosses the diagonal). The same computation for $U'=PR\cap KM$ gives the same ratio, so $U=U'$: $PR,KM,LN$ concur. By the same argument with the other diagonal, $QS,KM,LN$ concur; $KM$ and $LN$ meet in one point, so all four lines concur. ∎

**Application.** $ABA_1V$ is circumscribed about $\Gamma$ with tangency points $F$ on $AB$, $D$ on $BA_1\subset BC$, $X$ on $A_1V$, $E$ on $VA\subset AC$ (since $A_1$ lies on segment $DC$, $D$ is between $B$ and $A_1$, and $V$ lies between $E$ and $C$). By Newton, the diagonals $AA_1$ and $BV$ and the line $DE$ (joining the tangency points on the opposite sides $BA_1$ and $VA$) are concurrent. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p1b.title: Computation
pumac-2011-power-p1b.body:
Write $m=\frac{A_1B}{A_1C}$. The formula is symmetric under exchanging $B\leftrightarrow C$ (which replaces $m$ by $1/m$, $A_2B/A_2C$ by its reciprocal, and $s-b\leftrightarrow s-c$), so assume $A_1$ lies on segment $DC$, with $B,D,A_1,C$ in this order. Then $BA_1=\frac{ma}{1+m}$, $A_1C=\frac a{1+m}$ and
$$A_1D=BA_1-BD=\frac{ma}{1+m}-(s-b)=\frac{m(s-c)-(s-b)}{1+m}\ \ (a=(s-b)+(s-c)).$$
Let $V=A_1X\cap AC$ and, by (a), $S=AA_1\cap BV\cap DE$.

*First Menelaus.* In $\triangle AA_1C$ with the transversal $D,S,E$: $\frac{DA_1}{DC}\cdot\frac{EC}{EA}\cdot\frac{SA}{SA_1}=1$, i.e. $\frac{m(s-c)-(s-b)}{(1+m)(s-c)}\cdot\frac{s-c}{s-a}\cdot\frac{SA}{SA_1}=1$, so $\frac{SA}{SA_1}=\frac{(1+m)(s-a)}{m(s-c)-(s-b)}$.

*Second Menelaus.* In the same triangle with the transversal $B,S,V$: $\frac{BA_1}{BC}\cdot\frac{VC}{VA}\cdot\frac{SA}{SA_1}=1$, i.e. $\frac m{1+m}\cdot\frac{VC}{VA}\cdot\frac{(1+m)(s-a)}{m(s-c)-(s-b)}=1$, so $\frac{VA}{m(s-a)}=\frac{VC}{m(s-c)-(s-b)}=\frac{b}{mb-(s-b)}$ (their sum is $b$). Hence $VA=\frac{mb(s-a)}{mb-(s-b)}$ and $VE=VA-AE=\frac{(s-a)(s-b)}{mb-(s-b)}$.

*Third Menelaus.* In $\triangle A_1VC$ with the transversal $A,X,A_2$ ($A\in VC$, $X\in A_1V$, $A_2\in CA_1$): $\frac{AV}{AC}\cdot\frac{A_2C}{A_2A_1}\cdot\frac{XA_1}{XV}=1$. Here $XA_1=A_1D$ and $XV=VE$ (equal tangent lengths), so
$$\frac{m(s-a)}{mb-(s-b)}\cdot\frac{A_2C}{A_2A_1}\cdot\frac{m(s-c)-(s-b)}{1+m}\cdot\frac{mb-(s-b)}{(s-a)(s-b)}=1,$$
i.e. $\frac{A_2C}{(1+m)(s-b)}=\frac{A_2A_1}{m[m(s-c)-(s-b)]}$. These two numbers are proportional to the lengths $A_2C$, $A_2A_1$ whose sum is $A_1C=\frac a{1+m}$ ($A_2$ lies between $A_1$ and $C$), so both equal $\frac{a}{(1+m)[m^2(s-c)+(s-b)]}$. Thus $A_2C=\frac{a(s-b)}{m^2(s-c)+(s-b)}$, $A_2B=a-A_2C=\frac{am^2(s-c)}{m^2(s-c)+(s-b)}$, and $\frac{A_2B}{A_2C}=\frac{s-c}{s-b}m^2$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p1c.title: Ceva
pumac-2011-power-p1c.body:
Let $A_2=AX\cap BC$, $B_2=BY\cap CA$, $C_2=CZ\cap AB$. By (b) and its cyclic versions,
$$\frac{A_2B}{A_2C}=\frac{s-c}{s-b}\left(\frac{A_1B}{A_1C}\right)^2,\ \frac{B_2C}{B_2A}=\frac{s-a}{s-c}\left(\frac{B_1C}{B_1A}\right)^2,\ \frac{C_2A}{C_2B}=\frac{s-b}{s-a}\left(\frac{C_1A}{C_1B}\right)^2.$$
The product of the factors $\frac{s-c}{s-b}\cdot\frac{s-a}{s-c}\cdot\frac{s-b}{s-a}$ is $1$, and $\frac{A_1B}{A_1C}\cdot\frac{B_1C}{B_1A}\cdot\frac{C_1A}{C_1B}=1$ by Ceva for the concurrent cevians $AA_1,BB_1,CC_1$. So $\frac{A_2B}{A_2C}\cdot\frac{B_2C}{B_2A}\cdot\frac{C_2A}{C_2B}=1$, and $A_2,B_2,C_2$ lie on the sides (from the proof of (b), $A_2$ lies on the segment $BC$), so by Ceva's theorem $AX,BY,CZ$ are concurrent. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p2.title: Pascal twice
pumac-2011-power-p2.body:
Let $A_0=EF\cap YZ$. It suffices to show $A_0,C_1,B_1$ are collinear.

*Pascal on $F,F,E,Z,Z,Y$.* $A_1A_2\cap A_4A_5$ is the tangent at $F$ (the line $AB$) with the tangent at $Z$ (the line $C_1Z$): this is $C_1$. $A_2A_3\cap A_5A_6=FE\cap ZY=A_0$. $A_3A_4\cap A_6A_1=EZ\cap YF=:K$. So $C_1,A_0,K$ are collinear.

*Pascal on $E,E,F,Y,Y,Z$.* $A_1A_2\cap A_4A_5$ is the tangent at $E$ (the line $CA$) with the tangent at $Y$ (the line $B_1Y$): this is $B_1$. $A_2A_3\cap A_5A_6=EF\cap YZ=A_0$, $A_3A_4\cap A_6A_1=FY\cap ZE=K$. So $B_1,A_0,K$ are collinear.

Both $C_1$ and $B_1$ lie on the line $A_0K$, hence $A_0\in B_1C_1$ (if $K=A_0$ the statement follows by a limiting argument, or the lines coincide). The other two statements are the cyclic versions. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p3.title: Cross-ratios
pumac-2011-power-p3.body:
Let $K=BC_0\cap AC$. (We shall show $BK$ passes through $A_0$.)

*Step 1.* Project the line $BC$ onto $CA$ from $C_0$: $C\mapsto C$, $D\mapsto E$ (as $C_0\in DE$), $A_1\mapsto B_1$ (as $C_0\in A_1B_1$), $B\mapsto K$. By Lemma 2, $\frac{DC}{DB}:\frac{A_1C}{A_1B}=\frac{EC}{EK}:\frac{B_1C}{B_1K}$. (1)

*Step 2.* Ceva for the concurrent cevians $AD,BE,CF$ gives $\frac{AF}{FB}=\frac{AE}{EC}\cdot\frac{CD}{DB}$; Ceva for $AA_1,BB_1,CC_1$ gives $\frac{AC_1}{C_1B}=\frac{AB_1}{B_1C}\cdot\frac{CA_1}{A_1B}$. Dividing and using (1):
$$\frac{AF}{FB}:\frac{AC_1}{C_1B}=\frac{AE}{EC}\cdot\frac{B_1C}{AB_1}\cdot\left(\frac{CD}{DB}:\frac{CA_1}{A_1B}\right)=\frac{AE}{EC}\cdot\frac{B_1C}{AB_1}\cdot\frac{EC}{EK}\cdot\frac{B_1K}{B_1C}=\frac{AE}{EK}:\frac{AB_1}{B_1K}.$$
*Step 3.* So the cross-ratios of $A,F,B,C_1$ on $AB$ and $A,E,K,B_1$ on $AC$ are equal (with the common point $A$ corresponding to itself). By the converse of Lemma 2 the lines $FE$, $BK$, $C_1B_1$ are concurrent. But $FE\cap C_1B_1=A_0$, hence $A_0\in BK$. Since $K\in BC_0$ and $K\ne B$, the points $A_0,B,C_0$ are collinear. The other two statements are cyclic versions. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p4.title: Pascal
pumac-2011-power-p4.body:
Let $Q$ be the second point where line $A_0D$ meets $\Gamma$.

*Pascal on $Q,D,D,E,F,F$.* $QD\cap EF=A_0$; $DD\cap FF$ = tangent at $D$ ($BC$) $\cap$ tangent at $F$ ($AB$) $=B$; $DE\cap FQ=:R'$. So $A_0,B,R'$ are collinear. By Proposition 3, $A_0,B,C_0$ are collinear, so $R'$ and $C_0$ are both the intersection of the line $A_0B$ with $DE$: $R'=C_0$. Hence $Q$ lies on $FC_0$.

*Pascal on $F,Q,E,E,D,F$.* $FQ\cap ED=C_0$; $QE\cap DF=:R''$; $EE\cap FF$ = tangent at $E$ ($CA$) $\cap$ tangent at $F$ ($AB$) $=A$. So $C_0,R'',A$ are collinear. By Proposition 3, $A,B_0,C_0$ are collinear, and $B_0\in DF$, so $R''=B_0$. Hence $Q\in EB_0$.

Thus $A_0D$, $B_0E$, $C_0F$ all pass through $Q\in\Gamma$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p5a.title: Three Ceva products
pumac-2011-power-p5a.body:
Use signed ratios of directed segments on a line. Then for points $A'\in BC$, $B'\in CA$, $C'\in AB$ the lines $AA',BB',CC'$ are concurrent or all parallel iff $c_1=\frac{BA'}{A'C}\cdot\frac{CB'}{B'A}\cdot\frac{AC'}{C'B}=1$. Likewise (2) holds iff $c_2=\frac{B'A''}{A''C'}\cdot\frac{C'B''}{B''A'}\cdot\frac{A'C''}{C''B'}=1$ (Ceva in $\triangle A'B'C'$). Let $X=AA''\cap BC$, $Y=BB''\cap CA$, $Z=CC''\cap AB$; (3) holds iff $c_3=\frac{BX}{XC}\cdot\frac{CY}{YA}\cdot\frac{AZ}{ZB}=1$. We show $c_1c_2c_3=1$, which proves the theorem.

Apply the quadrilateral Menelaus theorem (Exercise $-8$; it holds for signed ratios, because $\frac{M_iA_i}{M_iA_{i+1}}$ is the ratio of signed distances to the line) to the quadrilateral $BCB'C'$ and the line $AA''$, which meets its sides $BC,CB',B'C',C'B$ at $X,A,A'',A$ (the point $A=CB'\cap C'B$ occurs twice):
$$\frac{XB}{XC}\cdot\frac{AC}{AB'}\cdot\frac{A''B'}{A''C'}\cdot\frac{AC'}{AB}=1 .$$
Since $\frac{BX}{XC}=-\frac{XB}{XC}$, this gives $\frac{BX}{XC}=-\frac{AB'}{AC}\cdot\frac{AB}{AC'}\cdot\frac{A''C'}{A''B'}$, and cyclically for $\frac{CY}{YA}$ and $\frac{AZ}{ZB}$. Multiply the three:
$$c_3=(-1)^3\left[\frac{AB'}{AC}\cdot\frac{CA}{CB'}\cdot\frac{BC'}{BA}\cdot\frac{AB}{AC'}\cdot\frac{CA'}{CB}\cdot\frac{BC}{BA'}\right]\cdot\left[\frac{A''C'}{A''B'}\cdot\frac{B''A'}{B''C'}\cdot\frac{C''B'}{C''A'}\right].$$
In the first bracket $\frac{AB'}{AC}\cdot\frac{CA}{CB'}=\frac{AB'}{B'C}$, $\frac{BC'}{BA}\cdot\frac{AB}{AC'}=\frac{BC'}{C'A}$, $\frac{CA'}{CB}\cdot\frac{BC}{BA'}=\frac{CA'}{A'B}$ (each after one sign change from reversing a segment), so the bracket is $\frac{AB'}{B'C}\cdot\frac{BC'}{C'A}\cdot\frac{CA'}{A'B}=\frac1{c_1}$. Each factor of the second bracket is $-$ the reciprocal of the corresponding factor of $c_2$, so the second bracket equals $-\frac1{c_2}$. Hence $c_3=(-1)^3\cdot\frac1{c_1}\cdot\left(-\frac1{c_2}\right)=\frac1{c_1c_2}$. So if two of $c_1,c_2,c_3$ equal $1$, so does the third. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p5b.title: Cevian nest
pumac-2011-power-p5b.body: Take the triangle $ABC$ with $A'=D$, $B'=E$, $C'=F$ on $BC,CA,AB$ and $A''=A_0$, $B''=B_0$, $C''=C_0$ on the lines $EF,FD,DE$ (the sides of $DEF$). Assertion (1): $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent (Gergonne point: Ceva with the tangent lengths $\frac{AF}{FB}\cdot\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}=\frac{s-a}{s-b}\cdot\frac{s-b}{s-c}\cdot\frac{s-c}{s-a}=1$). Assertion (2): $DA_0$, $EB_0$, $FC_0$ are concurrent (Proposition 4). By the cevian nest theorem, (3) holds: $AA_0$, $BB_0$, $CC_0$ are concurrent. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p6.title: Polars
pumac-2011-power-p6.body:
**Claim: $B_0C_0$ is the polar of $A_0$ with respect to $\Gamma$.**

(i) $A_0\in EF$, which is the polar of $A$ (the chord of contact of the tangents from $A$). By Lemma 4, $A$ lies on the polar of $A_0$.

(ii) For the four points $E,F,Y,Z$ of $\Gamma$ with $A_0=EF\cap YZ$, put $K_1=EZ\cap FY$ and $K_2=EY\cap FZ$. By the harmonic property of the complete quadrangle, the line $K_1K_2$ meets $EF$ at the harmonic conjugate of $A_0$ with respect to $E,F$, and $YZ$ at the harmonic conjugate of $A_0$ with respect to $Y,Z$; by the definition of the polar both lie on the polar of $A_0$. So the polar of $A_0$ is the line $K_1K_2$; in particular $K_1$ lies on it.

(iii) Pascal for the hexagon $F,D,E,Z,X,Y$: $FD\cap ZX=B_0$, $DE\cap XY=C_0$, $EZ\cap YF=K_1$ (Proposition 2). Hence $B_0,C_0,K_1$ are collinear.

(iv) By Proposition 3, $A,B_0,C_0$ are collinear. So the line $B_0C_0$ contains both $A$ and $K_1$, both of which lie on the polar of $A_0$. Therefore $B_0C_0$ is the polar of $A_0$. $\square$

The polar of $A_0$ is perpendicular to $IA_0$, so $IA_0\perp B_0C_0$: $I$ lies on the altitude from $A_0$. By the cyclic versions, $I$ lies on the altitudes from $B_0$ and $C_0$ as well. Hence $I$ is the orthocenter of $A_0B_0C_0$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p7.title: Cross-ratios
pumac-2011-power-p7.body:
Let $P_1=AB_0\cap BC$ ($=B_0C_0\cap BC$) and $P_2=CB_0\cap AB$ ($=A_0B_0\cap AB$).

*Perspectivity from $A_0$* (line $AC\to$ line $AB$): $A\mapsto A$, $R\mapsto S$, $B_1\mapsto C_1$ (since $A_0\in B_1C_1$), $C\mapsto P_2$ (since $A_0,B_0,C$ and $P_2$ are collinear). By Lemma 2, $(A,S,C_1,P_2)=(A,R,B_1,C)$.

*Perspectivity from $C_0$* (line $AC\to$ line $BC$): $C\mapsto C$, $R\mapsto T$, $B_1\mapsto A_1$ (since $C_0\in A_1B_1$), $A\mapsto P_1$ (since $A,B_0,C_0,P_1$ are collinear). So $(A,R,B_1,C)=(P_1,T,A_1,C)$.

Hence $(A,S,C_1,P_2)=(P_1,T,A_1,C)$ (cross-ratios of the four points on $AB$ and on $BC$).

*Perspectivity from $B_0$* (line $AB\to$ line $BC$): $A\mapsto P_1$ (as $A,B_0,P_1$ are collinear), $C_1\mapsto A_1$ (as $B_0\in C_1A_1$), $P_2\mapsto C$ (as $C,B_0,P_2$ are collinear). Let $S'=B_0S\cap BC$. By Lemma 2, $(A,S,C_1,P_2)=(P_1,S',A_1,C)$. Comparing with the previous equality, $(P_1,T,A_1,C)=(P_1,S',A_1,C)$, and since a cross-ratio determines the fourth point, $S'=T$. Thus $T\in B_0S$, i.e. $B_0$ lies on $ST$. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p8.title: Menelaus times Menelaus times Menelaus
pumac-2011-power-p8.body:
Use signed ratios. Menelaus in $\triangle AEF$ with the transversal $A_0,S,R$: $\frac{EA_0}{A_0F}\cdot\frac{FS}{SA}\cdot\frac{AR}{RE}=-1$. In $\triangle BDF$ with the transversal $B_0,S,T$: $\frac{FB_0}{B_0D}\cdot\frac{DT}{TB}\cdot\frac{BS}{SF}=-1$. In $\triangle CDE$ with the transversal $C_0,R,T$: $\frac{DC_0}{C_0E}\cdot\frac{ER}{RC}\cdot\frac{CT}{TD}=-1$. Ceva in $\triangle DEF$ for the concurrent lines $DA_0,EB_0,FC_0$ (Proposition 4): $\frac{EA_0}{A_0F}\cdot\frac{FB_0}{B_0D}\cdot\frac{DC_0}{C_0E}=1$.

Multiplying the three Menelaus relations and cancelling the Ceva product, and using $\frac{FS}{SF}=\frac{DT}{TD}=\frac{ER}{RE}=-1$:
$$-1=(-1)^3\cdot\frac{BS}{SA}\cdot\frac{AR}{RC}\cdot\frac{CT}{TB},$$
so $\frac{BS}{SA}\cdot\frac{CT}{TB}\cdot\frac{AR}{RC}=1$, i.e. $\frac{AS}{SB}\cdot\frac{BT}{TC}\cdot\frac{CR}{RA}=1$, which is Ceva's condition for $\triangle ABC$ and the points $S\in AB$, $T\in BC$, $R\in CA$. Hence $AT,BR,CS$ are concurrent (or parallel), i.e. $ABC$ and $TRS$ are perspective. ∎

pumac-2011-power-p9.title: Perspectivity
pumac-2011-power-p9.body: The triangles $ABC$ and $TRS$ are perspective (Proposition 8); here $T\in BC$, $R\in CA$, $S\in AB$. The points $A_0,B_0,C_0$ lie on $RS$, $ST$, $TR$ respectively and $AA_0,BB_0,CC_0$ concur (Proposition 5(b)). By the cevian nest theorem (applied to $ABC$, with $A'=T$, $B'=R$, $C'=S$ and $A''=A_0$, $B''=B_0$, $C''=C_0$) the lines $TA_0$, $RB_0$, $SC_0$ concur at a point $\Omega$: $A_0B_0C_0$ and $TRS$ are perspective.

pumac-2011-power-p9.title: The locus
pumac-2011-power-p9.body:
Let $P_1=B_0C_0\cap BC$ and $P_2=A_0B_0\cap AB$ (these do not depend on $R$) and $\ell=P_1P_2$. Since $ABC$ and $A_0B_0C_0$ are perspective, Desargues' theorem shows that $B_0C_0\cap BC=P_1$, $C_0A_0\cap CA=:O'$, $A_0B_0\cap AB=P_2$ are collinear; so $O'\in\ell$, and $O'=A_0C_0\cap AC$.

From Proposition 7's proof, the lines $AP_1$, $CP_2$, $ST$ pass through $B_0$, so the perspectivity from $B_0$ gives $(B,A,S,P_2)=(B,P_1,T,C)$. Project the points $B,A,S,P_2$ of line $AB$ from $O'$ onto the line $RS$: $B\mapsto A_0$ (as $O',B,A_0$ lie on $A_0C_0$), $A\mapsto R$ (as $O'\in AC$), $S\mapsto S$, $P_2\mapsto K:=\ell\cap RS$. So $(B,A,S,P_2)=(A_0,R,S,K)$. Similarly projecting $B,P_1,T,C$ from $O'$ onto the line $RT$: $B\mapsto C_0$, $P_1\mapsto L:=\ell\cap RT$, $T\mapsto T$, $C\mapsto R$. So $(B,P_1,T,C)=(C_0,L,T,R)=(T,R,C_0,L)$. Therefore $(A_0,R,S,K)=(T,R,C_0,L)$, i.e. (swapping the first two and the last two entries of both) $(R,A_0,K,S)=(R,T,L,C_0)$, on the two lines $RS$ and $RT$ through the common point $R$. By the converse of Lemma 2 the lines joining corresponding points, $A_0T$, $KL$ and $SC_0$, are concurrent. Their common point is $\Omega=A_0T\cap SC_0$, and $KL=\ell$. So $\Omega\in\ell$ for every position of $R$. Since $\Omega=RB_0\cap\ell$, and as $R$ runs along $AC$ the line $RB_0$ runs through all lines through $B_0$, $\Omega$ runs along the whole line $\ell$.

pumac-2011-power-p9.title: $\ell$ is tangent to the incircle
pumac-2011-power-p9.body: By Proposition 4 the lines $A_0D$, $B_0E$, $C_0F$ pass through $Q\in\Gamma$. Let the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $Q$ meet $BA$ at $M'$ and $BC$ at $N'$. The quadrilateral $M'N'CA$ is circumscribed about $\Gamma$ with tangency points $Q,D,E,F$ on $M'N',N'C,CA,AM'$. By Newton's theorem (see 1(a)) the diagonals $M'C$, $N'A$ and the lines $QE$, $DF$ are concurrent; but $QE\cap DF=B_0$ ($Q\in EB_0$). So $N'A$ passes through $B_0$, hence $N'=AB_0\cap BC=P_1$, and $M'C$ passes through $B_0$, hence $M'=CB_0\cap AB=P_2$. Therefore $\ell=P_1P_2=M'N'$ is the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $Q$. ∎
